chapter_title: The Apostle is asked: Why when you drew every thing in the Picture (- Book), did you not draw the Purification of the Catechumens who shall be cleansed by Transmigration?
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by institutional categories (catechumen/elect) and a hagiographic dialogue frame. The eschatological imagery (Judge, dispenser of justice, gehenna) is expressed in Christian-derived terms, and the explanation of transmigration is presented as catechumen instruction rather than impersonal cosmological system-mapping. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate is present at paragraph granularity.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Hagiographic scene-setting + Q&A set-up (“Once again… a catechumen stood up… he says to our enlightener”). This is editorial framing rather than systematic teaching.

Eschatological outcomes framed with Christian judicial/hell vocabulary (“Judge”, “dispenser of justice”, “gehenna”), presented as what is ‘depicted’ in the Picture-Book; this reads as Christian-overlay eschatological paraphrase rather than an internal cosmic-degree mapping.

Continues the same Christian-derived judicial/rest/afterlife register; rhetorical appeal to “see… face to face” in the Picture-Book. The catechumen question is anchored to church status and salvation staging, not to impersonal cosmological mechanics.

Dialogue attribution (“Then speaks the enlightener…”) plus catechetical explanation focused on the catechumen’s ‘path’ and its relation to ‘the elect’. Even where it gestures toward multiple ‘worlds’ and movements ‘from place to place’, it maps cosmos → church-category (catechumen/elect), so it functions as institutional instruction, not substrate exposition.

Explicitly institutional: contrasts “elect” and “catechumen,” and defines a ‘middle way of the purification of the catechumen’. The doctrine of varied purification locations is embedded in church discipline categories, indicating later pastoral/catechetical layer rather than the oldest cosmic correspondence teaching.
Formulaic narrative closure (“When that catechumen had heard… he was persuaded… kept silent”), matching the chapter-level ‘formulaic closing’ feature; typical editorial frame ending.
